headline: Meta launches new subscription tiers for businesses, creators, and AI power users
summary: Meta One plans range from $2.99/month to $499/month, combining exclusive features with expanded AI tool access.
details: Meta is expanding its paid offerings with a new lineup of "Meta One" plans targeting creators, businesses, and "AI power users." While core apps like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, along with Meta AI, will remain free, these new tiers offer additional benefits for a fee.

The subscription tiers include existing "single product plans" like Facebook Plus ($3.99/month) and Instagram Plus ($3.99/month), alongside new "bundle" options. These bundles combine benefits from the single product plans with enhanced Meta AI usage for tasks such as AI image and video generation, with options like the "Core" plan for $7.99/month and "Premium" for $19.99/month.

For creators and business owners, Meta One offers specialized plans starting at $14.99/month for "Essential." Higher-end business plans, such as "Advanced" for Instagram at $49.99/month, introduce features like scheduling Stories posts and embedding clickable URLs in captions. These plans also allow delegation of account access to multiple people without sharing passwords.

The top-tier "Max" plan is priced at $499/month and consolidates all previous benefits, offering the highest capacity for Meta's business agents. This plan also includes unlimited human support requests and the option for phone calls with company representatives.

Meta reports that its subscription plans have already seen significant traction, with over 15 million sign-ups and trial subscriptions. The company intends to extend subscription-based features to other products, including its video-editing app Edits and its AI glasses.

headline_marked: Police used [[jokes and gibberish]] to justify searching 19,000 Flock cameras
headline: Police used jokes and gibberish to justify searching 19,000 Flock cameras
summary: An EFF analysis revealed officers cited vague reasons and even 'LMAO' to justify widespread surveillance via automated license plate readers.
details: A new analysis by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has uncovered questionable practices in the use of Flock Safety's automated license plate reader (ALPR) network by law enforcement.

The EFF found that police officers searched through data from nearly 19,000 Flock cameras across 1,558 cities. The justifications provided for these searches were often vague, nonsensical, or even outright jokes.

In one instance, an officer reportedly used 'LMAO' as the reason for conducting a search, highlighting a concerning lack of accountability and transparency in how this powerful surveillance technology is being deployed.

This practice raises significant privacy concerns, as it suggests that the vast amount of data collected by these cameras may be accessed without legitimate investigative purpose, potentially leading to misuse and unwarranted surveillance of the public.
